questions.q: What does regularization add to the regression loss?
options: A bonus for larger coefficients
A penalty that grows with the size of the coefficients
Extra training rows
A second target column
questions.explain: The loss becomes squared errors plus alpha times a penalty on coefficient size, which discourages unnecessary complexity.

questions.q: What is the key practical difference between ridge and lasso?
options: Ridge only works on categorical data
Lasso needs no scaling and ridge does
They are identical for any alpha
Lasso can set some coefficients exactly to zero, while ridge only shrinks them
questions.explain: Lasso's absolute-value (L1) penalty can zero out coefficients, acting as feature selection. Ridge's squared (L2) penalty shrinks coefficients but rarely eliminates them.

questions.q: In the lesson's table, OLS scored 0.919 on training rows and -0.645 on test rows. What does that indicate?
options: Underfitting, because the score is negative
A bug in train_test_split
Severe overfitting: it fit the training noise and generalized worse than predicting the average
That the test set is too easy
questions.explain: A high training score with a negative test R-squared means the model memorized noise from 60 rows and 40 features. A negative R-squared means it does worse than always predicting the mean.

questions.q: Why is StandardScaler placed inside the pipeline before ridge or lasso?
options: Because penalties depend on coefficient size, which depends on feature units; scaling puts features on equal footing
Because it increases the number of features
Because it removes the need for a test set
Because lasso cannot run on unscaled numbers at all
questions.explain: A feature measured in large units gets a small coefficient and is penalized less. Standardizing makes the penalty treat features fairly, and fitting the scaler inside the pipeline avoids leakage.

questions.q: What is the right way to choose alpha?
options: Pick the value that gives the best score on the test set
Always use alpha = 1
Tune it with cross-validation on the training data, for example with RidgeCV or LassoCV
Set it to 0 so the penalty disappears
questions.explain: Alpha is a hyperparameter. Choosing it by test-set score leaks test information; cross-validation on training data, as RidgeCV and LassoCV do, keeps the test set honest.
